el: Ρε, μωρέ, άντε: τα μόρια του προφορικού λόγου
title: Particles, interjections and fillers of spoken Greek

blocks.title: The glue of spoken Greek
blocks.text:
Listen to two Greeks talking in a café and you will hear the content words (coffee, work, the landlord) wrapped in a constant layer of small words: **ρε**, **μωρέ**, **έλα**, **άντε**, **άσε**, **καλά**, **πω πω**, **δηλαδή**, **τέλος πάντων**. They carry almost no dictionary meaning, but they carry *attitude*: closeness, impatience, disbelief, sympathy, irony, the wish to change topic, the wish to stop being contradicted.

A B1 learner who speaks grammatically perfect Greek without them sounds like a news bulletin. A learner who sprinkles them randomly sounds like a parody. The goal of this unit is to know, for each one, **what attitude it signals, who you can use it with, and how it is said** (most of them change meaning with intonation).

Three things to keep in mind throughout:

1. **Intimacy scale.** Most of these words presuppose that you are on *εσύ* terms with the listener. With *εσείς* (strangers, elders, officials, your boss in a formal company) you drop ρε, μωρέ, βρε and the cheekier uses of έλα/άντε/άσε, and switch to *ορίστε, συγγνώμη, ξέρετε, βασικά, κοιτάξτε*.
2. **Tone is half the meaning.** *Καλά* can mean 'OK', 'fine, whatever' or 'are you serious?!'; *έλα* can mean 'hello', 'come on' or 'no way!'. The tables below give the tone for each use.
3. **Strength.** We use a 0-5 scale: 0 neutral, 1 casual, 2 slangy/cheeky, 3 rude, 4 vulgar/offensive, 5 taboo. Nearly everything here is 0-2; the few items that go higher are flagged and properly treated in the swearing and insults units.

blocks.title: How ρε actually works
blocks.text:
**Ρε** is the single most frequent marker of spoken Greek intimacy. It does three jobs:

- **Address**, before or after a name or noun: *Ρε Γιάννη!*, *Έλα ρε Μαρία!*, *Τι κάνεις ρε;* It is unstressed and leans on the next or previous word.
- **Emphasis on your own statement**: *Ναι ρε!* (Yes, really!), *Όχι ρε!* (No way / No, I'm telling you), *Σου λέω ρε!* (I'm telling you!).
- **Exasperation**: *Άντε ρε!*, *Έλα ρε!*, *Τι λες ρε;* Here ρε can be stressed and lengthened: *ρεεε*.

**Ρε συ** (literally 'hey you') softens a request or opens a confidence: *Ρε συ, μου δανείζεις ένα πεντάευρο;* With an aggressive tone (*Ρε συ! Πρόσεχε!*) it turns into a rebuke.

**Μωρέ** is the older, softer, more rural form. In modern speech it survives mostly in fixed combinations: *άσε μωρέ* (oh, forget it), *ναι μωρέ* (oh yes, of course, said dismissively or warmly), *έλα μωρέ* (oh come on), *μωρέ μπράβο!* (well done, you!). **Βρε** is the affectionate, slightly scolding, grandmotherly version; *βρε βρε βρε* (tsk tsk tsk) is what a yiayia says when you come home soaked.

**Feminine μωρή** is a different animal: between close female friends it is playful (*Μωρή τρελή!* you crazy girl!); from a man to a woman he does not know, or in an argument, it is insulting and old-fashioned-macho. In camp/gay slang it is a signature affectionate address. Learners should use it passively first.

blocks.text:
**Σιγά μην: the sarcastic 'as if'**

*Σιγά μην* + subjunctive (no να) is one of the most useful colloquial structures in Greek. It states that something will certainly **not** happen, with scorn:

- *Σιγά μην με πάρει τηλέφωνο.* As if he'd call me.
- *Σιγά μην πληρώσει αυτός.* Like he's ever going to pay.
- *Σιγά μην σκάσω!* As if I care! (lit. 'as if I'd burst')

It can stand alone as a reply: *— Θα σου ζητήσει συγγνώμη. — Ναι, σιγά!* (Yeah, right.) The polite equivalent is *Δεν νομίζω ότι…* or *Αμφιβάλλω αν…*.

blocks.title: Pronunciation and intonation
items: **ρε** is unstressed and attaches to its neighbour: *έλα ρε* is said as one word [ˈelare], *ναι ρε* [ˈnere]. Only when shouting (*Ρεεε!*) does it get its own stress.
**ρε συ** sounds like [reˈsi]; the συ takes the stress. Same with **ρε φίλε** [reˈfile].
**ντάξει** is εντάξει with the initial ε dropped (aphaeresis); ντ is [d]: [ˈdaksi]. Very common in fast speech and in texting (*ντξ*, *οκ*).
**τέλος πάντων** is run together and the ντ is voiced: [ˈtelospandon]; in fast speech even [ˈtelosˈpando].
**άσ' το, άσ' τα, άσ' με** drop the final ε of άσε: [ˈasto], [ˈasta], [ˈasme]. Likewise *πες το* [ˈpesto], *φέρ' το*.
**ας πούμε** [asˈpume], **να σου πω** [nasuˈpo], **που λες** [puˈles]: always one breath group.
**ξέρω 'γω** [ˈkseroɣo]: εγώ loses its ε after the vowel (prodelision), shown by the apostrophe.
**Έλα!** (disbelief) has a long, high first syllable that falls: *Έεελα!* **Έλα** answering the phone is bright and rising. **Έλα** = 'go on' is level.
**Καλά** with a falling tone = OK; short and clipped = annoyed 'fine!'; with rising tone + ρε = surprise.
**Πω πω** is usually two beats with a fall on the second (*ΠΩ πω*), lengthened for drama (*πωωω πω πω*). Never stressed on the second.
**ε;** at the end of a sentence rises like English 'eh?'. A level, held **εεε** is a hesitation; a short, falling **ε!** is a protest.
**Τσ** (the 'no' click) goes with a backward head tilt and raised eyebrows. A Greek 'no' can be completely silent: just the eyebrows.
Exasperation is shown by **lengthening the stressed vowel** and slowing down: *Άααντε!*, *Αμάααν!*, *Σιιιγά!*

items.en: A: Hi!

items.el: Β: Έλα ρε, τι κάνεις; Πού χάθηκες;
items.en: B: Hey man, how are you? Where did you disappear to?

blocks.title: Μωρός, μωρέ, ρε: from 'fool' to 'mate'
blocks.text:
**Ρε** has an interesting pedigree. Ancient Greek *μωρός* meant 'foolish' (cf. English *moron*), and its vocative *μωρέ* ('you fool!') was already a common, rough form of address in antiquity and Byzantium. Over centuries the insult wore away until *μωρέ* became a plain 'hey you', then shortened to *ωρέ* and *ρε*. The feminine *μωρή* kept more of its bite, which is why it still sounds cheeky or rude to a woman you are not close to.

In the 19th and early 20th century *ρε* was considered coarse, typical of the street, the port and the *μάγκες* of Piraeus. Today it is everywhere: in parliament off-mic, in sitcoms, in pop songs, between mothers and daughters. Greeks themselves joke that 'ρε' is a comma. Still, the old social line survives: you do not *ρε* your teacher, your doctor, an older stranger or a policeman. Doing so is either intimacy or aggression; there is no neutral middle.

*Άντε* comes from Turkish *haydi* 'come on', and the folksy form *άιντε* is common in songs (*Άιντε, ρε ζωή*). *Αμάν* is also Ottoman-era (Arabic *amān* 'mercy'), hence the *αμανέδες*, the improvised laments of rebetiko singers built around the cry *αμάν αμάν*.

Finally, *καλά κρασιά* ('good wines') was a sincere wish at grape-harvest time, when friends went round tasting the new wine. In modern speech it is almost always ironic: what you say when someone announces a plan you think is doomed, or when something has just gone predictably wrong.

**Common mistakes and false friends**

- **Ρε to the wrong person.** Saying *Ρε, πόσο κάνει;* to a shopkeeper you do not know is rude, not friendly. Use *Συγγνώμη, πόσο κάνει;* Same with *φίλε* to an older man: say *κύριε*.
- **Έλα on the phone to strangers.** *Έλα* presupposes you know who is calling. To an unknown number say *Ναι;*, *Παρακαλώ* or *Λέγετε* (old-fashioned).
- **Άσε! is not 'leave!'.** As a reply to *Πώς πήγε;* it means 'don't ask', i.e. it went badly. If you want someone to leave, that is *φύγε*.
- **Καλά! ≠ good!** On its own and clipped, *καλά!* is annoyed ('fine, whatever'). To praise something say *ωραία*, *τέλεια*, *μπράβο*.
- **Σιγά has two lives.** *Σιγά-σιγά* = slowly, little by little; *σιγά!* alone often = 'big deal'. *Σιγά μην* = 'as if'. Do not use *σιγά* to a stranger to mean 'slow down' with a sharp tone: it sounds dismissive.
- **Μπα ≠ no in every context.** *Μπα* is a casual, slightly doubtful 'nah'. In a formal answer or to an elder say *όχι* or *δεν νομίζω*.
- **Δηλαδή can be aggressive.** *Δηλαδή;* alone, with a hard rise, means 'Meaning what, exactly?' and can sound like a challenge.
- **Μωρή from a man.** Leave it to Greek women and to comedy for now.
- **Over-use.** Native speakers do not put ρε in every sentence of a calm conversation. Two or three particles per exchange is natural; ten sounds like a sketch show.

blocks.title: Φωνητικό μήνυμα: η πρόταση στο γραφείο
blocks.text:
Μαράκι, έλα, εγώ είμαι. Σου αφήνω φωνητικό γιατί δεν το σηκώνεις, ως συνήθως. Άκου να δεις τι έγινε σήμερα, δεν θα το πιστέψεις.

Πάω λοιπόν, που λες, το πρωί στη δουλειά, και βλέπω τον Αντώνη στην είσοδο με ένα τεράστιο μπουκέτο. Λέω, ωχ, ποιος πέθανε; Τίποτα, μου λέει, για τη Δέσποινα από το λογιστήριο. Έλα ρε! Ναι ρε! Της κάνει πρόταση, λέει, μπροστά σε όλους, στο διάλειμμα. Πω πω, λέω, θάρρος!

Τέλος πάντων, έρχεται το διάλειμμα. Μαζευόμαστε όλοι στην κουζίνα, δήθεν για καφέ. Μπαίνει η Δέσποινα, ο Αντώνης γονατίζει, ε, και αρχίζει έναν λόγο, ας πούμε πέντε λεπτά, για τη μοίρα και τα αστέρια, ξέρω 'γω. Εμείς σιωπή. Και η Δέσποινα; Τον κοιτάει, κοιτάει και το μπουκέτο, και λέει: «Ρε συ Αντώνη, εγώ είμαι αλλεργική στα κρίνα».

Μπα, δεν τελειώνει εκεί. Μετά από ένα λεπτό λέει: «Κοίτα, να σου πω, εντάξει, ναι». Ναι! Πω πω πω, χειροκροτήματα, φωνές, ο προϊστάμενος να λέει «Άντε, και στα δικά μας!». Αχ, πολύ γλυκό ήταν, δηλαδή, τι να λέμε.

Εντωμεταξύ, η Λίτσα δίπλα μου μουρμουρίζει: «Καλά κρασιά. Σιγά μην κρατήσει έναν χρόνο». Της λέω: «Άσε μωρέ, άσ' τους να χαρούν». Και μου κάνει: «Καλά, καλά, θα δεις».

Ουφ, κάπως έτσι πέρασε η μέρα. Δουλειά, βέβαια, δεν έγινε καθόλου. Ο Αντώνης κερνούσε γλυκά σε όλο τον όροφο, η Δέσποινα έδειχνε το δαχτυλίδι σε όποιον περνούσε, κι εγώ, ρε παιδί μου, κλείστηκα στην τουαλέτα και έκλαψα σαν χαζή. Ε, όχι και κάθε μέρα πρόταση γάμου!

Άντε, πάρε με όταν μπορείς, γιατί έχω κι άλλα κουτσομπολιά. Και μην πεις «θα σε πάρω» και χαθείς πάλι, ε; Σε ξέρω. Έλα, φιλάκια, γεια!
blocks.en:
Mara dear, hi, it's me. I'm leaving you a voice message because you're not picking up, as usual. Listen to what happened today, you won't believe it.

So I go to work in the morning, you see, and I see Antonis at the entrance with a huge bouquet. I think, uh-oh, who died? Nothing, he tells me, it's for Despina from accounts. No way! Yes, really! He's proposing to her, he says, in front of everyone, at the break. Wow, I say, guts!

Anyway, the break comes. We all gather in the kitchen, supposedly for coffee. Despina walks in, Antonis kneels down, well, and starts a speech, say five minutes long, about fate and the stars, I dunno. Us, total silence. And Despina? She looks at him, looks at the bouquet, and says: 'Antonis, hon, I'm allergic to lilies.'

Nope, it doesn't end there. After a minute she says: 'Look, to be honest, OK, yes.' Yes! Oh my god, applause, shouting, the manager going 'Here's to us next!'. Ah, it was really sweet, honestly, what can I say.

Meanwhile Litsa next to me mutters: 'Well, good luck with that. As if it'll last a year.' I tell her: 'Oh, come on, let them be happy.' And she goes: 'Yeah, yeah, you'll see.'

Phew, that's more or less how the day went. Work, of course, didn't happen at all. Antonis was handing out sweets on the whole floor, Despina was showing the ring to anyone who walked past, and me, for heaven's sake, I locked myself in the toilet and cried like an idiot. Well, it's not every day there's a marriage proposal!

Go on, call me when you can, because I've got more gossip. And don't say 'I'll call you' and vanish again, OK? I know you. Right, kisses, bye!
